title: The NAACP
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of the NAACP (National Association for the Advancement of Colored People), from its founding in 1909 after the Springfield, Illinois race riot, through its early legal victories like Guinn v. United States, its anti-lynching campaign (including the Waco Horror and the Dyer Bill), its role in Brown v. Board of Education and the Little Rock Nine, its civil rights era achievements, and its post-civil rights struggles, including the 2004 IRS investigation, membership and finance troubles, and the six Game Changers. The episode closes with a listener mail segment from a six-year-old listener.
topics: National Association for the Advancement of Colored People
Central High School Little Rock desegregation

segments.title: Opening banter and NAACP name
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode and discuss how people say N-double-A-C-P and the debate over whether the name should change, and the organization's current reinvention focusing on economic equality.

segments.title: Springfield riot and founding of the NAACP
segments.summary: The August 1908 Springfield, Illinois riot, triggered by the arrest of two men, is described, with deaths, displacement and unpunished violence. W. E. B. Du Bois and about forty others, mixed race and religion, met in New York in 1909, first as the National Negro Committee, then renamed NAACP in 1910.

segments.title: NAACP charter and legal strategy
segments.summary: The hosts read the NAACP's founding charter goals, including equality of rights, suffrage and equal justice, and explain its court-focused strategy alongside direct action. Early leaders included Moorfield Storey and Florence Kelley.

segments.title: Press strategy and early supporters
segments.summary: The NAACP sought press coverage because lynchings went unreported; it founded The Crisis magazine, and Oswald Garrison Villard used his publishing connections to publicize such events.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A short break before the next segment.

segments.title: Guinn v. United States and grandfather clauses
segments.summary: The NAACP's challenge to Oklahoma's grandfather clause led to the Supreme Court overturning it in 1915 in Guinn v. United States. The hosts discuss state's rights and federal intervention in voting discrimination.

segments.title: Birth of a Nation boycott and anti-lynching push
segments.summary: The NAACP boycotted the film Birth of a Nation, which brought mainstream publicity. The group refocused on federal anti-lynching legislation after the 1916 lynching of Jesse Washington in Waco, Texas, and its investigator's report, the Waco Horror.

segments.title: Dyer Bill, anti-lynching bills and Emmett Till Antilynching Act
segments.summary: The Dyer Bill passed the House but died in the Senate after a Southern Democrat filibuster. About two hundred anti-lynching bills died in Congress by mid-century. In June 2020 the Emmett Till Antilynching Act passed the Senate and House but stalled when Rand Paul objected to the bill's bodily injury language. The Senate apologized in 2005 for failing to outlaw lynching. The NAACP flew a flag reading a man was lynched yesterday.

segments.title: Lynching and racial violence in the 1910s
segments.summary: Lynchings averaged more than one per week over the period. Mob violence included burning black neighborhoods, such as the 1917 St. Louis race massacre, triggered by a black family moving into a white neighborhood.

segments.title: Civil rights era, Brown v. Board and Little Rock Nine
segments.summary: During the civil rights era the NAACP litigated, lobbied and registered voters, and Rosa Parks was a Montgomery NAACP secretary. Thurgood Marshall argued Brown v. Board of Education. In 1957 Governor Faubus called in National Guard troops to block the Little Rock Nine at Central High; Eisenhower sent federal troops, the 101st Airborne, to enforce integration.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A short break before the final content segments.

segments.title: Post-civil rights era, finances and IRS investigation
segments.summary: After the 1960s legislation, the NAACP faced questions about relevance. Its finances struggled, with layoffs in 2007 and near bankruptcy in the 1970s. In 2004 the IRS investigated its nonprofit status over a speech criticizing President Bush; the IRS dropped the probe. Governance, a sixty-four member board and branch restrictions were criticized.

segments.title: Six Game Changers and current work
segments.summary: In 2011 the NAACP announced six Game Changers: economics, sustainability, education, health, public safety and criminal justice, voting rights and political representation, and youth engagement. Current activities include protests, litigation and lobbying, with about half a million members and more than two thousand branches.

segments.title: Listener mail from a six-year-old
segments.summary: A six-year-old listener named Christopher from Toronto writes in praising episodes on origami, Monopoly and peanut butter, and asks for a Harry Potter episode. The hosts thank him and give the email address.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the episode and give the show's contact email.
